questions.stem: The three global WIND SYSTEMS are the Trade Winds, Westerlies, and Polar Easterlies. Which wind system is responsible for the Indian MONSOON?

options.option_text: Polar Easterlies
Trade Winds
Jet streams only
Westerlies

questions.explanation: PERMANENT WINDS: (1) TRADE WINDS — blow from sub-tropical HIGH (30°N/S) towards the equatorial LOW (0°). Northeast Trades (N hemisphere) + Southeast Trades (S hemisphere). CORIOLIS EFFECT deflects them. Named 'Trade' because they helped sailing ships in colonial 'trade'. (2) WESTERLIES — blow from 30° to 60° latitude. Come from the west. Stronger in S hemisphere ('ROARING FORTIES', 'FURIOUS FIFTIES', 'SCREAMING SIXTIES' — due to fewer landmasses). (3) POLAR EASTERLIES — blow from polar highs toward sub-polar lows. INDIAN MONSOON = a DIFFERENTIAL HEATING phenomenon — in summer, the Indian subcontinent's massive landmass heats up faster than the Indian Ocean → LOW PRESSURE over land + HIGH PRESSURE over sea → the SE trades cross the equator (deflected to SW monsoon by Coriolis) and blow moist air onto the subcontinent (June-September). In winter, REVERSE: land cold → high pressure → NE monsoon blows dry air OUTWARD from land to sea. Monsoon is technically a SEASONAL REVERSAL of winds. reversed as monsoon in summer.
questions.subject: Geography

_fixes.was: Trade Winds (reversed as monsoon in summer)

questions.stem: The 'LOO' is a hot, dry wind experienced in which region, during which season?

options.option_text: Himalayan foothills; winter
Northwest India (Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, UP, Delhi)
Coastal Tamil Nadu; monsoon
Central Maharashtra; spring

questions.explanation: LOO — a hot, dry, dusty wind blowing westerly/northwesterly over the PLAINS of northwestern India + Pakistan. Mostly May-June. Temperatures 45-50°C. Can cause heat strokes. Plants wilt; groundwater dries. Contrary to normal afternoon cooling, Loo afternoons are the hottest. Other LOCAL WINDS in India: (1) KALBAISAKHI / NORWESTERS — sudden violent thunderstorms in WB + Assam pre-monsoon (April-May). Also called 'Bardoli Chheerha' in Assam. Brings relief from heat + some rain for tea crops. (2) MANGO SHOWERS — pre-monsoon summer showers in KA, Kerala, Coastal AP (April-May) — help mango flowering, hence the name. (3) BLOSSOM / CHERRY BLOSSOM SHOWERS — Kerala, KA post-picking summer showers on coffee plantations (April-May — similar). (4) ANDHI — hot dust storms in Rajasthan. WORLD LOCAL WINDS: CHINOOK (Rockies, warm + dry — 'snow-eater'), FOEHN (Alps — analogous), MISTRAL (France, cold N wind), SIROCCO (N Africa, hot dry), HARMATTAN (W Africa, dry), ZONDA (Andes), SIMOOM (Arabia), KHAMSIN (Egypt), BORA (Adriatic, cold NE), BRICKFIELDER (Aus, hot dry). summer (May-June).

questions.stem: The CHINOOK wind — warm + dry, known as the 'SNOW-EATER' — blows down the leeward side of which mountain range?

options.option_text: Alps in Europe
Rocky Mountains in North America
Andes in South America
Himalayas

questions.explanation: CHINOOK — warm, dry wind on the EASTERN (leeward) slopes of the ROCKY MOUNTAINS in the USA + Canada. Can raise temperatures by 20-30°C within hours (especially in winter), melting snow rapidly — hence 'SNOW-EATER'. Forms when a moist Pacific air mass rises on the western slopes (loses moisture as rain/snow), then descends dry on the eastern slopes — compression heats it (adiabatic warming: ~10°C/km for dry air). Similar FOEHN WINDS occur worldwide on leeward sides: FOEHN (Alps — German original name, which 'chinook' loosely translates), CHINOOK (Rockies), BERG (South Africa), ZONDA (Andes). KATABATIC WINDS — cold winds flowing downhill by gravity (denser cold air) — include MISTRAL (Alps → Rhone valley → Mediterranean, cold NW, France), BORA (Dalmatia coast, cold NE from Balkans to Adriatic), FALL WINDS on Antarctic coast. HURRICANES / CYCLONES / TYPHOONS: region-specific names for the same phenomenon — tropical cyclones. Atlantic + NE Pacific = 'hurricane'; NW Pacific = 'typhoon'; Indian Ocean + South Pacific = 'cyclone'.

questions.stem: The CORIOLIS FORCE — an APPARENT force caused by Earth's rotation — deflects winds (and ocean currents) to the RIGHT in the Northern Hemisphere and to the LEFT in the Southern Hemisphere. Where is Coriolis effect ZERO?

options.option_text: North Pole
At the EQUATOR
Tropic of Cancer
At 45° latitude

questions.explanation: CORIOLIS EFFECT — an apparent deflection of moving objects (air, water, projectiles) as observed from a rotating frame (Earth). Magnitude proportional to sin(latitude) × velocity × 2ω (ω = Earth's angular velocity). ZERO at the EQUATOR (latitude 0°). MAXIMUM at the POLES (latitude 90°). In N Hemisphere: deflects to the RIGHT. In S Hemisphere: deflects to the LEFT. CONSEQUENCES: (1) Tropical cyclones rotate counterclockwise in N and clockwise in S hemispheres; (2) They DON'T form within ~5° of the equator (too little Coriolis); (3) Trade winds deflect from northward/southward to become NE trades (N hem) + SE trades (S hem); (4) Bullet trajectories curve over long distances. Named after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis (French, 1835). Myth: toilet/sink water drains in opposite directions N vs S hemispheres — FALSE for small basins (effect too weak; drain direction depends on basin shape).

questions.stem: The Indian SUMMER MONSOON enters India from which direction, and which branch is formed by the Western Ghats' orographic effect?

options.option_text: NE direction; Arabian Sea branch
SOUTHWEST direction; ARABIAN SEA branch strikes Kerala first (~1 June), Western Ghats force uplift → heavy rain on windward slopes
West direction; Bay of Bengal branch
Easterly; from China

questions.explanation: INDIAN SUMMER MONSOON (SW Monsoon, June-September) has TWO BRANCHES from the Indian Ocean: (1) ARABIAN SEA BRANCH — strikes Kerala coast first around 1 June (official 'monsoon onset'). Moves up the west coast, hits WESTERN GHATS which force it to rise → OROGRAPHIC / RELIEF RAIN on the windward (western) slopes — Mahabaleshwar, Amboli, Agumbe (Karnataka's 'Cherrapunji of the South' — ~7000 mm/year), Western Ghats spine. Rain shadow (leeward side) → Deccan plateau gets much less rain. (2) BAY OF BENGAL BRANCH — reaches NE India first, deflected by Arakan Yoma + Meghalaya hills → strikes Khasi Hills (MAWSYNRAM — Earth's wettest place, ~11,872mm/year; CHERRAPUNJI — #2). Then curves up Ganga plain from east to west. ONSET dates (normal): Kerala 1 June → Mumbai 10 June → Delhi 27 June → NW India/Punjab 1 July. WITHDRAWAL: reverse order, starting NW India early September to full withdrawal by mid-October. IMD officially records monsoon start/end dates every year.

questions.stem: The 'ROARING FORTIES', 'FURIOUS FIFTIES', and 'SCREAMING SIXTIES' refer to:

options.option_text: Nautical miles per hour
Strong WESTERLIES in the SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE between 40°-60° latitudes
Speeds of Indian monsoon winds
Colours of sea at different depths

questions.explanation: 'ROARING FORTIES' (40-50°S), 'FURIOUS FIFTIES' (50-60°S), 'SCREAMING SIXTIES' (60-70°S) — strong westerly winds in the SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE Mid-latitudes. These winds are much more intense than their N hemisphere counterparts because: (1) less LAND in S hemisphere to create friction (90% of mid-latitude S hem is OCEAN — big open water bodies); (2) more uninterrupted fetch → winds build up. Sailors historically used Roaring Forties for SW Passage / fast east-bound voyages around the Cape of Good Hope (Africa) or Cape Horn (S America). Still dangerous for shipping. Home to many famous ocean disasters. In N hemisphere, the 40-60° zone is mostly LAND (Eurasia + N America), so winds are moderated. The ANTARCTIC CIRCUMPOLAR CURRENT (ACC) — driven by these westerlies — is the largest ocean current in the world (~125 Sverdrups). Also called the 'WEST WIND DRIFT'. No continents obstruct it.

options.option_text: Latitudes near the equator with no winds (Doldrums)
SUBTROPICAL HIGH PRESSURE belts at ~30° N/S where winds are CALM / variable and descending air causes DRY conditions
Latitudes where horses naturally migrate
Polar regions

questions.explanation: HORSE LATITUDES — 30° N and 30° S latitudes — regions of SUBTROPICAL HIGH PRESSURE, where air descends (from equatorial ascent) and winds are CALM / light / variable. Descending air is COMPRESSED + WARMED → LOW HUMIDITY → clear skies + DRY conditions. Home to MOST of the world's great DESERTS: Sahara (Africa, 30°N), Thar (India), Arabian (Arabia), Gobi (Mongolia, slightly higher), Mexican, Great Victoria (Aus), Kalahari + Namib (S Africa, 30°S), Patagonian, Atacama (Chile). NAME ORIGIN: Sailing ships would be becalmed here for weeks — to save water, sailors threw HORSES (cargo) overboard. Also called the 'Calms of Cancer/Capricorn'. Adjacent zones: EQUATORIAL CALMS = DOLDRUMS / ITCZ (Intertropical Convergence Zone) — where trade winds meet, low pressure, ascending air, heavy rains (equatorial rainforests: Amazon, Congo, Indonesian). Polar regions also have SUBSIDING cold air → dry (Antarctica = technically largest desert). POLAR FRONTS at 60° latitude — low pressure, stormy — birthplace of mid-latitude cyclones. most deserts here.

questions.stem: The SAHARA DESERT in Africa is kept extremely dry due to which major atmospheric feature?

options.option_text: Ocean currents only
Subtropical HIGH PRESSURE belt at ~30°N (Horse Latitudes) causing descending dry air
Rain shadow of the Rockies
Polar vortex influence

questions.explanation: SAHARA DESERT dryness: primarily due to the SUBTROPICAL HIGH PRESSURE BELT at ~30°N latitude (Horse Latitudes) — subsiding dry air from the HADLEY CELL circulation. Sahara sits right under this zone. Secondary factors: cold CANARY CURRENT off the west African coast (cold water → less evaporation → less rain over land); huge distance from moisture sources (interior Africa); Atlas Mountains + Red Sea create additional barriers. Sahara is ~9.2 million km² — larger than continental USA — and the 3rd-largest desert globally (after Antarctic + Arctic polar deserts). HOTTEST recorded temperature on Earth: Furnace Creek, Death Valley (56.7°C, 1913) — though some Sahara sites have come close. HADLEY CELL — tropical atmospheric circulation cell from 0° to ~30°; responsible for tropical rains AND subtropical deserts (0°=rising, 30°=sinking). FERREL CELL (30°-60°) + POLAR CELL (60°-90°) — other global circulation cells. IRONY of Sahara: used to be a lush savannah with lakes as recently as 6000 years ago (Holocene Green Sahara).

questions.stem: The HARMATTAN is a dry, dusty wind that blows across West Africa and is sometimes called the 'doctor wind' by coastal communities. In which direction does it blow, and where does it originate?

options.option_text: Southwest to northeast, originating off the Atlantic Ocean
Northeast to southwest, originating from the Sahara Desert
Northwest to southeast, off the Mediterranean coastline
East to west, driven by the Indian Ocean monsoon system

questions.explanation: The Harmattan blows from the northeast to the southwest — it is a dry continental trade wind that originates over the Sahara and blows toward the Gulf of Guinea coast of West Africa. It is called the 'doctor wind' because its dryness provides relief from the humid equatorial air. Option A reverses the direction; the Atlantic-origin wind in West Africa is the moisture-bearing South-West Monsoon, not the Harmattan.

questions.stem: Sailors historically called the equatorial calm belt the 'DOLDRUMS'. Which modern meteorological description BEST explains both its name (calm winds) and its characteristic weather (heavy rain)?

options.option_text: Sub-Polar Low Belt; cold polar air rises and diverges poleward
Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone; intense convective uplift of heated air
Subtropical High Pressure Belt; descending dry air near 30° latitude
Polar Front Zone; collision of polar air and mid-latitude westerlies

questions.explanation: The Doldrums correspond to the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) near the equator. The NE and SE trade winds converge here, and intense solar heating drives strong vertical (convective) uplift. This vertical motion means there is minimal horizontal pressure gradient — hence calm surface winds — yet the rising air cools, condenses, and produces heavy rainfall. Option C (Subtropical High at 30°) is the opposite: it is a zone of descending air and clear skies, not calm equatorial belt.

questions.stem: The POLAR FRONT JET STREAM significantly steers mid-latitude weather systems. At approximately what altitude does it flow, and in what general direction?

options.option_text: 2–5 km altitude, flowing primarily from east to west
10–12 km altitude, flowing broadly from west to east
15–20 km altitude, flowing from the equator poleward
5–8 km altitude, flowing from the poles toward the equator

questions.explanation: Jet streams form near the tropopause at roughly 9–12 km altitude where strong horizontal temperature gradients exist. The Polar Front Jet Stream flows from west to east (westerly) in both hemispheres due to the Coriolis effect. Option A (east-to-west) confuses jet streams with trade winds, which do flow easterly at low altitude in the tropics; jet streams are upper-tropospheric and westerly in mid-latitudes.

questions.stem: The SIROCCO wind originates as a hot, dry wind over the Sahara Desert. What transformation does it undergo as it crosses the Mediterranean Sea toward southern Europe?

options.option_text: Remains hot and dry throughout; sea moisture is absorbed by convection aloft
Starts hot and dry over the Sahara, becomes hot and humid crossing the sea
Starts cold and moist off the Atlas Mountains, warms through compression
Begins as a cold northerly from the Alps, intensifies over North Africa

questions.explanation: The Sirocco (also spelled Scirocco) forms as a hot, dry wind blowing northward from the Sahara. As it traverses the Mediterranean Sea, it picks up significant moisture from the water surface, arriving in southern Italy, Malta, and the Balkans as a hot, oppressive, humid wind. Option A is incorrect — the relatively cool Mediterranean Sea cannot 'absorb' moisture upward into a passing wind; the wind absorbs moisture from below. Option D describes the Mistral, not the Sirocco.

questions.stem: The Mediterranean climate (Csa/Csb) is uniquely characterised by hot DRY SUMMERS and mild WET WINTERS. Which atmospheric mechanism DIRECTLY explains the dry summer season?

options.option_text: Polar jet stream shifts equatorward, blocking Atlantic moisture in summer
Subtropical high pressure belt migrates poleward, suppressing rainfall
Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone moves into Mediterranean latitudes
Monsoon low-pressure trough draws moisture toward the equator in summer

questions.explanation: The seasonal migration of pressure belts is the key mechanism. In Northern Hemisphere summer, the Sun's direct overhead position migrates northward, causing pressure belts to shift poleward. The subtropical high-pressure belt (centred around 30°N in winter) migrates to approximately 35–40°N, bringing its subsiding, dry air over Mediterranean regions — suppressing convection and blocking westerly cyclones. In winter it retreats, and the westerlies bring rain. Option A (jet stream blocking moisture) is a partial distractor; the jet stream does shift, but it is the subtropical HIGH, not the jet stream, that is the primary driver.

questions.stem: During a LA NIÑA event, how does the WALKER CIRCULATION change, and what is the typical consequence for Australian rainfall compared to neutral years?

options.option_text: Walker Circulation weakens; central Pacific warms; Australia faces drought
Walker Circulation strengthens; upwelling off Peru increases; Australia gets wetter
Walker Circulation reverses; cold upwelling shifts to western Pacific; India dries
Walker Circulation collapses; Atlantic trade winds strengthen; India stays unaffected

questions.explanation: La Niña is characterised by anomalously cool sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. This steepens the temperature gradient across the Pacific, intensifying the Walker Circulation — the east-to-west overturning cell. Stronger trade winds push more warm water toward the Indo-Pacific Warm Pool, enhancing convection and rainfall over Australia and Southeast Asia, while increasing cold upwelling off the South American coast. Option A describes El Niño conditions, not La Niña. Option C incorrectly states that the Walker Circulation reverses — reversal characterises El Niño, not La Niña.

questions.stem: In the THREE-CELL MODEL of global atmospheric circulation, the FERREL CELL is described as a 'thermally indirect' cell. Which statement BEST explains this characterization?

options.option_text: It is driven by direct solar heating, similar to the thermally direct Hadley Cell
It is mechanically forced; warm air descends at 30° and cold air rises at 60°
It exists only in the Northern Hemisphere due to continental asymmetry
It is thermally direct because warm equatorial air rises within it and sinks poleward

questions.explanation: A thermally direct cell has warm air rising and cold air sinking — as in the Hadley Cell (warm equatorial air rises) and Polar Cell (cold polar air sinks). The Ferrel Cell is the opposite: warm air descends at the subtropical high (~30° latitude) and relatively cooler air rises at the subpolar low (~60° latitude). This counter-intuitive circulation is maintained not by thermal buoyancy but by mechanical momentum transferred from the adjacent Hadley and Polar cells, making it 'thermally indirect'. Option D conflates the Ferrel Cell with the Hadley Cell; Option C is factually wrong — Ferrel Cells exist in both hemispheres.
